items.title: Lexplain – AI-powered Linux kernel change explanations
items.raw_excerpt: To understand what changed between kernel versions, you have to dig through the git repository yourself. Commit messages rarely tell you the real-world impact on your systems — you need to analyze the actual diffs with knowledge of kernel internals. For engineers who use Linux — directly or indirectly — but aren't kernel developers, that barrier is pretty high. I kept finding out about relevant changes only after an issue had already hit, and it was most frustrating when the version was too new to find similar cases online. I built lexplain with the idea that it would be nice to quickly scan through kernel changes the way you'd skim the morning news. It reads diffs, analyzes the code, and generates two types of documents: - Commit analyses: context, code breakdown, behavioral impact, risks

items.title: Origin – Git blame for AI agents (track which AI wrote every line)
items.raw_excerpt:
We built Origin after realizing nobody on our team could answer "which AI wrote this?" when a bug appeared. Origin hooks into Claude Code, Cursor, Gemini, and Codex. Every commit gets tagged with which agent wrote it, what prompt generated it, which model, and what it cost. Run `origin blame` on any file and you see [AI] or [HU] per line — like git blame but for AI agents. All data stored in git notes. No server required, works offline, zero lock-in. CLI is open source (MIT): github.com/dolobanko/origin-cli
Team dashboard: getorigin.io Would love feedback on the attribution approach — we're using git notes to store session data on commit hashes.

Over the past two years, large models with hundreds of billions of parameters have emerged one after another. However, for the vast number of small and medium-sized enterprises, AI solutions that rely on expensive servers and complex network environments remain out of reach. Meanwhile, policy trends are also shifting. Government departments have intensively introduced supporting policies to encourage technology companies to develop "lightweight, low-cost, and easy-to-deploy" intelligent solutions. Driven by the "AI+" initiative, empowering thousands of industries with AI has evolved from an optional choice to a mandatory task.

Yet market pain points are equally acute. Network conditions in district and county markets vary widely, with weak IT infrastructure and limited budgets; traditional channel partners face intensified competition and shrinking profit margins; small and medium-sized business owners are stuck in the dilemma of "wanting to use AI but unable to afford or effectively utilize it." These practical issues make the "last mile" of AI a challenge the entire industry must confront directly.

Against this backdrop, Dahua Technology presented its answer at the 2026 Channel Local Operation Partner Conference: firmly adhering to the "local operation, district and county penetration" channel strategy, and leveraging edge intelligence + scenario customization to bridge the "last mile" of AI implementation. Dahua Technology President Zhao Yuning stated frankly at the conference, "Small and medium-sized scenario-based projects have become one of the new growth engines in the industry." As large projects in first-tier cities approach saturation, district and county markets are becoming the true blue ocean for intelligent transformation. However, this blue ocean must be unlocked with lighter, more flexible, and more grounded approaches.

excerpt_i18n.en: Imagine a robot reaching for a cup on a table, lifting it slightly, then pausing, returning it to its original position, and reaching for it again. It repeats the same action as if forgetting what it just did. Similar scenarios are common in real-world environments: repeatedly pressing a button that has already been pressed, or continuing to push a drawer that is already closed. These failures are not due to an inability to "see clearly," but rather a lack of a "world model" capable of simulating the evolution of time and space. While current vision-language-action models can understand images and instructions, they still rely solely on current observations for decision-making in continuous tasks. Once tasks become long-step processes, such as picking up an object, moving it, placing it, and then closing a device, issues like repeated actions and decision interruptions arise, fundamentally due to a lack of temporal understanding. This problem is becoming a critical bottleneck in the development of embodied intelligence. Most existing methods are based on an immediate reaction mechanism of "do what you see," which performs well in short tasks but often leads to incoherent actions and decision drift in long-sequence tasks. Enabling models not only to perceive the current state but also to remember the past and anticipate the future has become a new core challenge. In this context, the team led by Wang Donglin at Westlake University proposed the paper *HiF-VLA: Hindsight, Insight and Foresight for Vision-Language-Action Models*.
excerpt_i18n.es: Imagina que un robot extiende su brazo para tomar una taza sobre la mesa, la levanta, se detiene, la devuelve a su lugar y luego vuelve a intentar tomarla. Repite la misma acción como si olvidara lo que acaba de hacer. Situaciones similares son comunes en entornos reales: presionar repetidamente un botón que ya ha sido activado, o seguir empujando un cajón que ya está cerrado. Estos fallos no se deben a que "no vea bien", sino a la falta de un "modelo del mundo" capaz de simular la evolución del espacio-tiempo. Aunque los modelos actuales de visión, lenguaje y acción pueden comprender imágenes e instrucciones, en tareas secuenciales aún dependen únicamente de observaciones inmediatas para tomar decisiones, lo que se vuelve problemático cuando las tareas se alargan.

Many people have experienced this: asking an AI to draw a character results in a first image that looks great, but the second one starts to differ slightly, and by the third, it’s practically a different person. When tasked with creating a set of posters, each individual piece may be fine, but together they lack stylistic consistency. Or, when generating storyboard frames, the character’s appearance fluctuates—sometimes heavier, sometimes slimmer—with facial features failing to match across images. Even a simple change like adjusting clothing color might inadvertently alter the face as well. These may seem like minor issues, but in real-world applications, they can be critical. In fields such as IP design, brand visuals, content production, and even industrial and medical scenarios, the requirement is never just for a single attractive image, but for consistency across an entire set.
